source.title: Memorisation bias in medical AI
source.authors: Moritz A. Knolle; M. Menten; Laurin Lux; Mélanie Roschewitz; Emma A. M. Stanley; G. Kaissis; D. Rueckert; Ben Glocker

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a patient's historical records alter predictions on that patient's future records and diagnostic accuracy. It does not test random-label fitting, the train-test gap, or any of the specific measures in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The study reports longitudinal prediction shifts and diagnostic-accuracy changes when a patient's historical records are included in training. These are related to memorisation but do not measure any version's specified behavior. Cited prior-work claims about generalization and memorisation capacity are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures how including patients' historical records changes predictions on their unseen future records. It does not test any specified version. In particular, its inclusion/exclusion design neither selects the most-memorized examples for removal nor compares their removal with random removal, as V8 requires. References to memorization supporting generalization are prior-work claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Historical-record inclusion can alter predictions on patients' unseen future records. In simulated diagnostic analyses restricted to records with detected memorization effects, these changes often reduced sensitivity for de novo conditions and increased sensitivity and specificity for unchanged states. Patient-level DP suppressed these effects more effectively than record-level DP. Actual downstream clinical harm and its deployment incidence remain unquantified.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised medical classification and patient-level record inclusion/exclusion comparisons to measure longitudinal prediction shifts, not random-label memorization or the train-test generalization gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and model architecture changed the frequency and magnitude of detected future-record prediction shifts. Record-level versus patient-level differential privacy changed the observed memorisation. The study reports that effects generally become rarer and weaker over longer acquisition intervals.

fits_no_version.finding: Historical-record inclusion significantly changed future predictions for 2.25% of random-forest records, 0.04% of logistic-regression records, and 0.12% of tabular-ResNet records; maximum changes were 16.7, 1.2, and 10.2 percentage points, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on patients' historical records can alter predictions on their unseen future records, with frequency and magnitude depending on model architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Among future records selected for detected memorization effects, historical-record inclusion reduced sensitivity for many de novo conditions and increased sensitivity and specificity for many unchanged conditions; not every condition showed a significant difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longitudinal memorization can impair detection of new conditions while increasing diagnostic accuracy for unchanged health states among affected returning contributors.

fits_no_version.finding: Patient-level DP nearly eliminated detected future-record effects, whereas record-level DP left significant effects even at ε = 1. DP training also reduced held-out diagnostic performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Patient-level privacy protection can suppress longitudinal memorization more effectively than record-level protection, with utility costs dependent on the implementation.

record.problems: The diagnostic-harm analysis is simulated, not prospective; the authors say de novo cases are rare and longer follow-up estimates rest on comparatively few records. Patient-level DP used a naive implementation that discards all but one record per patient, confounding privacy cost with data loss. Some reported outcomes are presented in figures without exact text values.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports numerous condition-specific sensitivity and specificity comparisons in Fig. 4, Extended Data Figs. 3–5, and DP diagnostic performance and memorisation counts in Fig. 5. They are omitted because they are outside V1–V8 and the figure-only values cannot be reliably assigned as exact row values from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Controlled dropout comparisons, including training-set size and augmentation interactions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing the most-memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and measuring retrained test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures fit no version; this does not deny the reported longitudinal effects. Omitted diagnostic comparisons are declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries for these versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps around and beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-model generalization.
Large- versus small-batch generalization under epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures of the train-test gap.
Selecting the most-memorized examples for removal and comparing retraining with random-example removal.

rows.subject: random forest
rows.operation_detail: Compared predictions on future records from models trained with versus without each patient's historical records.
rows.measure: Future records with significant prediction changes
rows.locator: Results, “Memorisation alters future predictions”; Extended Data Fig. 1d-f
rows.note: Significance was assessed by comparing model groups partitioned by patient inclusion.
rows.check: The reported 2.25% (1,469/65,402) is correct; random partitioning detected zero affected records. This measures longitudinal prediction changes, not a V1–V8 effect.

rows.subject: logistic regression model
rows.operation_detail: Compared predictions on future records from models trained with versus without each patient's historical records.
rows.measure: Future records with significant prediction changes
rows.locator: Results, “Memorisation alters future predictions”; Extended Data Fig. 1d-f
rows.note: The study reports this rate was lower than for the random forest and tabular ResNet.
rows.check: The reported 0.04% (25/65,402) is correct. Its smaller rate than the random forest does not establish partial occurrence of any claim version.

rows.subject: tabular ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared predictions on future records from models trained with versus without each patient's historical records.
rows.measure: Future records with significant prediction changes
rows.locator: Results, “Memorisation alters future predictions”; Extended Data Fig. 1d-f
rows.note: The study reports this rate was lower than for the random forest.
rows.check: The reported 0.12% (83/65,402) is correct. This tabular architecture comparison does not measure convolutional versus fully connected generalization on images.

rows.subject: random forest
rows.operation_detail: Measured prediction-change effect size on future records.
rows.note: Effect size is the absolute difference in average predicted probability.
rows.check: The 16.7 percentage-point maximum is correct. Specify that the effect is the maximum across diagnostic classes of the absolute difference between group-mean probabilities; it measures no claim version.

rows.subject: logistic regression model
rows.operation_detail: Measured prediction-change effect size on future records.
rows.note: Effect size is the absolute difference in average predicted probability.
rows.check: The 1.2 percentage-point maximum is correct, but its small magnitude is not a partial V1–V8 effect.

rows.subject: tabular ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Measured prediction-change effect size on future records.
rows.note: Effect size is the absolute difference in average predicted probability.
rows.check: The 10.2 percentage-point maximum is correct, but it measures longitudinal prediction changes rather than any claim version.

rows.subject: models trained with record-level DP
rows.operation_detail: Trained using record-level differential privacy and compared predictions for patient-inclusion versus patient-exclusion model groups.
rows.value: Substantial share of historical and future records still showed significant changes
rows.locator: Results, “Risk mitigation via differential privacy”; Fig. 5a&c
rows.note: The text gives no exact counts here; it reports effect sizes on future records at the largest tested budgets exceeding 40 percentage points for both datasets.
rows.check: Residual significant changes at record-level DP ε = 1 are supported. Their detection compares patient-inclusion and patient-exclusion groups; non-private models provide the mitigation comparison. The over-40-point effects in the note concern larger ε budgets, not necessarily ε = 1. Neither result measures a claim version.

rows.subject: models trained with patient-level DP
rows.operation_detail: Trained using patient-level differential privacy and compared predictions for patient-inclusion versus patient-exclusion model groups.
rows.measure: Future records with significant prediction changes
rows.locator: Results, “Risk mitigation via differential privacy”; Fig. 5a
rows.note: The text says patient-level DP essentially did not transfer historical-record memorisation to future records.
rows.check: Counts 0, 0, 0, 2 are correct. The authors characterize future-record effects as essentially absent and effect-size distributions as near random-partitioning baselines. The extracted partial state does not describe any V1–V8 effect.

rows.subject: models trained with patient-level DP
rows.operation_detail: Trained using patient-level differential privacy and compared predictions for patient-inclusion versus patient-exclusion model groups.
rows.value: No significant changes across tested budgets in either historical or future records
rows.locator: Results, “Risk mitigation via differential privacy”; Fig. 5c
rows.note: The authors report no detected significant prediction changes for HEEDB under patient-level DP.
rows.check: No significant changes under patient-level DP on HEEDB are correctly reported, but this absence concerns longitudinal memorization bias, not a claim version.

rows.subject: models trained with patient-level DP
rows.operation_detail: Compared diagnostic performance of patient-level DP models with matched non-private baselines.
rows.locator: Results, “Risk mitigation via differential privacy”; Fig. 5b&d
rows.note: The authors caution that this utility cost may be overestimated because their patient-level approach discarded all but one record per patient.
rows.check: Specify the measure as held-out macro-average AUROC. DP utility loss does not test V8: records were retained by recency for patient-level protection, not removed by memorization ranking with a random-removal control. Matched non-private baselines used the same data; distinguish privacy loss relative to those baselines from data loss relative to full-record training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
